summary: Specifies the 'ippget' pull delivery method for IPP event notifications, building on RFC 3995. The client asks the printer for notifications rather than having them pushed.

eli5.summary: Instead of the printer calling you, you ask now and then whether it has news.

questions: what is the ippget delivery method
what is event wait mode in ipp
how do ipp printers send event notifications
subtitle: How an IPP client asks a printer for its event notifications, either by polling or by holding a connection open.

tldr.problem: IPP printers can raise events such as job completion, and RFC 3995 needs at least one agreed way to get those notifications to the client that wants them.
tldr.mechanism: The Printer stores each Event Notification for a set time. The client then pulls them with a new Get-Notifications operation, either as one request or by keeping the connection open (Event Wait Mode) so the Printer can stream more as events occur.
tldr.outcome: The 'ippget' method is REQUIRED for every client and Printer that supports RFC 3995. It uses ordinary IPP over HTTP in the same direction as other IPP requests, so it adds no new firewall considerations.

today: RFC 3996 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2911 and defines the delivery method that RFC 3995 requires.

sections.title: A Pull Method for Printer Events
sections.content:
This RFC adds to Internet Printing Protocol 1.1 (RFC 2911). It defines the 'ippget' Pull Delivery Method for the event notification framework of RFC 3995. The Notification Recipient acts as a client and fetches (pulls) Event Notifications with a new operation, Get-Notifications.

The method is REQUIRED for all clients and Printers that support RFC 3995. When an Event occurs, the Printer saves the Event Notification for a period called the Event Life. The client can then ask for everything held for one or more Subscription objects.

The RFC says the method is designed mainly for two cases: a client that wants Events for a job it submitted (from the job's Per-Job Subscription object), and a privileged client that wants all job or printer Events from a Per-Printer Subscription object.
sections.eli5: The printer keeps a notebook of things that happened. You come by and ask to read it, instead of the printer chasing you down.

sections.title: How Pulling Works
sections.content:
A client picks this method by sending notify-pull-method with the keyword value ippget when it creates a Subscription. From then on, the Printer MUST generate an Event Notification for each Event, assign it the Event Life and hold it for that long.

To collect notifications the client sends Get-Notifications with the subscription ids it cares about. The Printer returns every un-expired Event Notification held for them. A Printer MUST accept the request in any printer state and MUST stay in the same state.

For a Per-Job Subscription, the client typically sends Get-Notifications within a second of creating the Subscription. Because the Printer MUST keep Event Notifications for at least 15 seconds, it is unlikely to miss anything that happened in between.

If the caller lacks the required access rights, the Printer MUST reject the request with client-error-forbidden, client-error-not-authenticated or client-error-not-authorized, as appropriate.
sections.eli5: You tell the printer which job you are following, and it hands over every note it still has about that job.

sections.title: The Get-Notifications Request and Response
sections.content:
The request carries three notable operation attributes. notify-subscription-ids lists the Subscriptions and needs at least one value. notify-sequence-numbers gives the lowest sequence number wanted for each one, so the client does not get the same notifications twice; missing values are treated as 1. notify-wait is a boolean that requests Event Wait Mode.

The Printer can answer in three ways. If it is too busy it returns server-error-busy and the notify-get-interval attribute. If the client did not ask for Event Wait Mode, the Printer returns what it holds right away, plus notify-get-interval, the number of seconds after which the client SHOULD ask again. If the client asked for Event Wait Mode, the Printer returns what it holds and keeps sending more as Events occur, until the Subscriptions are canceled.

The Printer MAY end Event Wait Mode at any time by returning notify-get-interval, and the client MUST accept this and disconnect. Each response also carries printer-up-time, and one Event Notification Attributes Group per matched notification, in ascending time stamp and sequence number order.
sections.eli5: You can ask once and get an answer with a note saying when to come back, or stay at the counter while the clerk reads you new notes as they arrive.

sections.title: Event Wait Mode and Transport
sections.content:
The encoding is modeled on the Get-Jobs response in RFC 2911. Each Event Notification Attributes Group starts with the event-notification-attributes-tag (hex 0x07) and ends with an end-of-attributes-tag.

Without Event Wait Mode, the response ends like any other IPP response. With Event Wait Mode, the Printer returns the response as an application/ipp part inside a multipart/related MIME type, and sends each later Event as another application/ipp part.

Proxy servers may delay some Event Notifications or cause time-outs, so a client MUST be prepared to perform Get-Notifications again when a time-out occurs. If a client fails to receive a response, it can ask for the same notifications again and gets those that have not expired in the meantime.
sections.eli5: When you stay on the line, the printer reads out each new note as a separate message in one long phone call.

sections.title: Event Life, Status Codes and New Values
sections.content:
The Printer description attribute ippget-event-life is the number of seconds after an Event during which the Printer will return it. It MUST be 15 or more, and 60 seconds is the RECOMMENDED value. A Printer MUST also keep completed, canceled or aborted Job objects in the Job Retention or Job History phases for at least that long.

The value of notify-get-interval MUST be at least as large as ippget-event-life, so a client that waits the full interval will not miss events.

The RFC adds the operation id 0x001C for Get-Notifications and the status code successful-ok-events-complete (0x0007). That status tells the client this is the last response for a Subscription: it was canceled, it was deleted when a Per-Printer lease expired, or the job-completed event occurred for a Per-Job Subscription.
sections.eli5: The printer promises to keep each note for at least 15 seconds, and it tells you with a special message when there will be no more news.

sections.title: Who Must Support What
sections.content:
Supporting IPP Notifications is OPTIONAL. But a Printer or client that supports RFC 3995 MUST support the 'ippget' method.

A conforming Printer MUST support Get-Notifications including Event Wait Mode, the ippget-event-life attribute, the new values and the new status code. It MUST listen for Get-Notifications requests on the IANA-assigned well-known port 631 unless an administrator or site policy configures otherwise, and SHOULD NOT listen on any other port.

A conforming client MUST create Subscriptions using notify-pull-method with ippget (not notify-recipient-uri), send requests to the port in the 'ipp' URL or otherwise to port 631, and convert 'ipp' URLs to their 'http' forms for the HTTP layer.
sections.eli5: If a printer or computer talks about notifications at all, it must know this one basic way to do it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method adds no new security mechanisms and relies on those of IPP/1.1. Its access control matches Get-Job-Attributes, except that it targets Subscription objects. The caller MUST be the owner of the Subscription, an operator or administrator of the Printer, or otherwise authorized by the administrator's security policy.

Because Get-Notifications travels in the same direction as job creation, usually from the same client, the RFC says it poses no additional authentication, authorization, privacy, firewall or port assignment issues. Since the recipient starts every request, there is also no chance of unwanted push notifications (spam).

One caveat remains. A client gets all events for a Subscription in the requested range, not only those it wants. A client that subscribes to a job event on a Per-Printer Subscription could receive events from thousands of other jobs, so the RFC suggests a Per-Job Subscription to protect itself.
sections.eli5: Only you can ask for your own notes, and nobody can flood you since you start every conversation. Follow just your own job so you are not buried in other people's news.
